transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-18
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Chris Alvarez (Evergreen IT), Elena Park (Evergreen Security), Sam Ortega (Evergreen CTO), Priya Singh (Evergreen Cloud)

Summary: discovery focused on Private/VPC deployment options. Main topics: VPC peering vs Private Endpoints, egress/ingress controls, region constraints, KMS and audit logs, deployment timeline and pilots.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan Lee from Redwood, joined by Maya our solutions engineer. How's it going at Evergreen?
[00:08] Sam (CTO): Hey Jordan, thanks for doing this. Busy week but excited to dig into the private hosting options.
[00:12] Priya (Cloud): Hi all. We're mostly focused on networking and compliance today.
[00:16] Jordan (AE): Great. Maya, do you want to kick off with a quick overview?
[00:20] Maya (SE): Sure, quick 5 minute. So Redwood supports three hosting modes — hosted API, dedicated reserved pools, and private deployments into your VPC or private network. For the private option we offer a customer-managed control plane or a private data plane depending on the model. The core ask we usually see is how we connect: VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink/private endpoints, or transit gateway setups.
[00:45] Elena (Security): Can you explain the difference between peering and private endpoints again? I sometimes see the terms mixed.
[00:52] Maya (SE): Yeah absolutely. VPC peering is basically a direct route between two VPCs, lowest latency and simplest routing, but you need peering between each Redwood VPC and your VPC; that can be N squared if you have many regions. PrivateLink or private endpoints uses an interface endpoint in your VPC and we expose an NLB in our side — it simplifies routing and hides our side's IPs. Also works well with shared services in a hub-and-spoke setup.
[01:18] Chris (IT): Sounds good. Our concern is egress IPs — we need a fixed set for allowlisting with some of our partners. Can you provide static egress IPs?
[01:25] Maya (SE): For private deployments we can publish the NAT or egress IPs you need to allowlist. In Dedicated or Private you can also use a NAT gateway under your control so egress is entirely on your side. If we deploy into your VPC (bring-your-own-vpc model) then you control outbound IPs.
[01:40] Sam (CTO): Region question: we have data residency requirements — some customers must stay in eu-west-1. Can you run the private data plane in eu-west-1?
[01:47] Jordan (AE): Yes, we support region-constrained deployments. For Private we can provision in the region you ask for, subject to capacity. Maya, do you want to add technical nuance?
[01:55] Maya (SE): Right — we have standard AMIs and kube/serving stacks tested in major regions. For a private on-prem or VPC install in eu-west-1 we can provision either a VPC peering setup or PrivateLink depending on your preference. A quick caveat is custom hardware/quantization variants might need special kernel support, but for most open models we support eu-west-1.
[02:13] Elena (Security): Auditability — we need full request logs, token-level billing, and KMS integration. Is audit logging available in Private?
[02:20] Maya (SE): Yes, Private includes audit logs shipped to your CloudWatch/S3/GCS depending on provider. We also support CMEK via your KMS or HSM for key management on Private. For Hosted we have a multi-tenant KMS design but can't give you customer-managed keys unless you go Private.
[02:36] Chris (IT): Are there performance implications with PrivateLink vs peering? We care about latency for some synchronous features.
[02:42] Maya (SE): In our benchmarks peering typically has lower latency because traffic stays within the cloud fabric. PrivateLink adds an extra hop through the interface endpoint and NLB, typically 2-5 ms overhead. For most workloads it's fine, but for sub-10ms SLOs peering is preferable.
[02:59] Sam (CTO): I heard something about KV cache and larger seq lengths impacting memory — how does that change our infra needs?
[03:05] Maya (SE): Good question — our runtime uses KV cache to speed up generation; longer sequences require more memory per request. If you expect long-context usage we recommend larger GPU types or a mix of batching policies. We'll share model profiles for memory and sequence performance.
[03:19] Priya (Cloud): On the VPC side, our security team wants to avoid opening inbound ports from the internet. Will the Redwood nodes require inbound rules?
[03:26] Maya (SE): If we do a peering deployment, the peering is private and you won't need public inbound rules. For PrivateLink, you'll create an interface endpoint that talks to our NLB — no internet-facing inbound. If we host the data plane entirely in your account, we won't require any public ingress.
[03:40] Elena (Security): For compliance, we need SOC 2, ISO, penetration test reports and also the right to audit logs. Can you provide those?
[03:46] Jordan (AE): Yes, we'll share SOC 2/ISO certs and pen-test summaries. For Private deployments you get access to raw audit logs and we can sign an addendum for audit rights. We'll send that pack after the call.
[03:57] Chris (IT): Network specifics — what ports and IP ranges do you need opened for peering or PrivateLink?
[04:03] Maya (SE): We'll provide a network checklist. Generally for peering you don't open ports; routing tables need entries for our subnets. For PrivateLink you'll open the interface endpoint which will consume ENIs in your subnets; the NLB on our side talks TLS 443 to the endpoint. For some model variants we use gRPC on 443 or 8443 in rare cases, but TLS always. We'll enumerate the exact ports and security groups in the checklist.
[04:28] Sam (CTO): Ok timeline wise, if we want a pilot in May — what's realistic?
[04:33] Jordan (AE): If we get network info and the signed PO, a pilot in 2-3 weeks is doable. Maya: any infra prep?
[04:38] Maya (SE): We'll need your VPC CIDR, subnet IDs for the endpoints, and an admin with network permissions. If peering, create a peering request and share the peering connection id. For PrivateLink, create the interface endpoint subnets and the security groups. We'll provide precise steps.
[04:55] Priya (Cloud): We might have to route via our transit gateway — will that complicate things?
[04:59] Maya (SE): Transit gateway is fine; you can attach the interface endpoints or peering routes through TGW. We have customers using hub-and-spoke. The only caution is cross-account route propagation timing — sometimes it takes a few minutes to converge.
[05:13] Elena (Security): Encryption at rest for model cache and logs — is that CMEK?
[05:17] Maya (SE): Yes, CMEK supported on Private. Logs and model artifacts can be encrypted with your key. For Hosted, we use provider-managed keys.
[05:25] Chris (IT): Ok, minor note — our partner integrator needs static egress IPs for webhooks. If you can't provide static IPs from your side we'll need to egress through our NAT.
[05:33] Jordan (AE): Both options exist. We can provide a published list of egress ranges, or we can deploy the compute in your VPC so your NAT controls egress. We'll include both approaches in the architecture doc.
[05:44] Sam (CTO): Pricing — ballpark difference between Dedicated and Private?
[05:47] Jordan (AE): Dedicated is reserved capacity on Redwood-managed infra — lower per-token cost at scale, but less control over keys and networking. Private includes the extra work to run in your VPC or private cloud and has a platform fee plus infra cost. We'll send a comparative pricing sheet.
[06:02] Priya (Cloud): Any constraints on region availability? If we want multiple regions behind a failover, how do you handle multi-region private deployments?
[06:09] Maya (SE): We can provision multi-region private deployments, but each region is an independent deployment that we can tie together with smart routing. For automatic failover we recommend DNS-based routing with health checks or an active-active approach with stateful sync for KV caches — that gets more complex. We'll map out options.
[06:26] Elena (Security): Are you able to restrict admin console access to IP ranges or SSO only?
[06:31] Maya (SE): For Private you can integrate SAML/SSO with role-based access and lock down console to your IP allowlist. For Hosted we support SSO but IP lockouts are more limited.
[06:41] Chris (IT): Any gotchas with route tables and overlapping CIDRs?
[06:44] Maya (SE): Overlapping CIDRs are a blocker for peering. For PrivateLink it's less of an issue since interface endpoints use ENIs in your subnets. If you have overlaps we can recommend NAT/proxy approaches but simplest is non-overlapping CIDRs.
[06:58] Sam (CTO): One more question — telemetry and costs: can we get per-route token-level billing?
[07:03] Maya (SE): Yes, Private comes with token-level cost breakdowns per model/route, and you can export to your billing system. Also trace IDs for request-level debugging.
[07:12] Jordan (AE): Alright, we're nearing the end. Quick recap of next steps?
[07:16] Jordan (AE): We'll send (1) architecture + network checklist, (2) SOC2/ISO pack + KMS details, (3) preliminary pricing sheet for Dedicated vs Private, (4) propose a network deep-dive for 2027-04-22.
[07:29] Priya (Cloud): That sounds good. Also we'll gather the VPC details and get back to you.
[07:33] Elena (Security): Please include the pen-test summary and any third-party audit schedules.
[07:37] Jordan (AE): Will do. Anything else from Evergreen?
[07:40] Chris (IT): No, that's it. Thanks.
[07:42] Jordan (AE): Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with docs and a calendar invite for the network call.
[07:47] Sam (CTO): Thanks.
